sources.note: Silent. Sec. 3.3 'Southern Muji phonology in brief' (pp. 8-9): {(C)(V)VT} template, segment inventory, 'five pitch contrasts: high-level /55/, mid-level /33/, low-rising /13/, low-falling /21/ and, high-falling /52/', sandhi [22-21]/[22-21-21], tense voice as co-articulation of /21/ and /13/, non-contrastive nasalization. sources.citation: Pelkey, Jamin R. 2007. Muji's mirrored merger: correlative redistribution of checked tone classes in a newly defined Burmic cluster. Mon-Khmer Studies 37: 179-195.
sources.access_detail: open copy posted by the author (located 2026-09-25); a digital copy (available on request)
sources.quote: Tone. Muji-PJZ has five contrastive tones 55, 33, 13, 21, 52-illustrated in Figures 2 and 3 below with nasal and stop initial contrasts respectively. Transcriptions are intended to indicate allotonic pitch values relative to the F0 increments to the left of the pitch plots || Of these four tonemes, 52 is the most marginal. Muji varieties often feature this pitch as an allotone of the low falling toneme 21, the high-level toneme 55, and/or the low-rising toneme 13-via sandhi induced phenomena. Accordingly, in PJZ this pitch value can also be spotted masquerading as toneme 21 or 55 via sandhi rules: /21/ > [52]: / __ 55; /21/ > [52] ~ [31]: / __ 13; /55/ > [52]: / __ 21 + 52. Contrastive environments are well-established, however, and include cases of tonemic fusion. || Regarding other Muji tonemes, the 13 tone class in PJZ (and in many other varieties) is often realized with contour shapes such as [213] [212] and [313]. [...] Some varieties possibly feature a 22 contrast, but this pitch value usually only surfaces due to sandhi in Muji: /21/ > [22]/ __ 21 unless three 21 tones are in succession in which case /21, 21, 21/ > [22, 21, 21] or [21 22 21] depending on the variety.
sources.locator: printed p. 182 and printed p. 183, sec. 2 Sample phonology sketch, Figures 2-3
sources.note: Silent. Sec. 2 'Sample phonology sketch' (pp. 181-183) describes Muji-PJZ (= Southern Muji, Pujiazhai): syllable C(V)VT, 34 initials, 9 monophthongs + 9 diphthongs, five contrastive tones 55/33/13/21/52 with pitch plots, sandhi rules (/21/>[22] before 21, /21/>[52] etc.), phonation non-contrastive but co-occurring with tones 21 and 13. No mention of stress, accent or prominence anywhere in the article (scanned a full-text search for stress/accent + pages read).

sources.citation: Pelkey, Jamin R. 2006. Muji uncorked: A first tasting of the dialects, distinctives and distribution. Paper presented at the 39th International Conference on Sino-Tibetan Languages and Linguistics (ICSTLL 39), University of Washington, Seattle, 15-17 September 2006. [Conference abstract, 1 p., archived at web.archive.org/web/20080905074627/http://depts.washington.edu/icstll39/abstracts/icstll39_pelkey.pdf;full paper/handout not located.]
sources.note: The paper defines the Muji dialect cluster by shared phonological, morphological and lexical innovations, and names as the first of these 'a correlative redistribution of the *Ngwi tonal split that points back to a intermediate merger' (i.e. the checked-tone-class 'mirrored merger' later published as Pelkey 2007 MKS 37 = a work listed here and in rows 6-7); it also gives 'a sample phonology sketch of a Muji dialect spoken in Jinping County' (Southern Muji, not Phuma), plus demography, maps, emerging dialect boundaries and endangerment notes.
